Olympia. A sacred sanctuary in the western Peloponnese dedicated to Zeus, it was the religious and athletic center of the Greek world for over a thousand years. The birthplace of the Olympic Games, the greatest athletic competition in antiquity, Olympia embodied the Greek ideals of competition, physical excellence, and religious devotion.

Olympia hosted the Olympic Games every four years without interruption for nearly 1,200 years, from 776 BCE to 393 CE. These games attracted athletes and spectators from across the Greek world. The sanctuary was built to honor Zeus, featuring the Temple of Zeus and the Statue of Zeus, a gold-and-ivory masterpiece by Phidias that was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

The sculpture of Zeus by Phidias stood over 40 feet tall and was seated within the temple. It was so magnificent that visitors wept upon seeing it. Olympia housed the Altis, a sacred grove containing temples, treasuries, and votive monuments built by city-states to commemorate their victories.

The Olympic truce, called the Ekecheiria, suspended all warfare during the games. Even enemies agreed to peace so that athletes could compete safely. Victory was honored with olive wreaths, not gold. Victory itself was the supreme prize, bringing honor and prestige to the champion's home city far more than any material reward could offer.

The remains of the sanctuary, buried by earthquakes and floods over the centuries, were discovered by archaeologists in the nineteenth century and extensively excavated. Zeus was the chief deity honored at Olympia. The Olympic Games were the athletic competition held every four years at the sanctuary. Phidias was the sculptor of the massive statue of Zeus. Pausanias, an ancient geographer, described Olympia's monuments in extraordinary detail in his writings.
